kartellrecht-grundlagen-01.question: What three categories of conduct does the cartel prohibition under Sec. 1 GWB cover?

options.a: Only written contracts between competitors
options.b: Agreements, decisions by associations of undertakings, and concerted practices
options.c: Only price-fixing in retail trade
options.d: Only conduct by dominant undertakings

kartellrecht-grundlagen-01.explanation: Sec. 1 GWB prohibits agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings, and concerted practices that have the object or effect of preventing, restricting, or distorting competition - almost identical wording to Art. 101(1) TFEU. Important: the mere object (not only an actual effect) is sufficient.

kartellrecht-grundlagen-02.question: What does the "object or effect" wording in Sec. 1 GWB mean for so-called hardcore restrictions (e.g. price-fixing)?

options.a: Actual economic harm must always be proven
options.b: The agreement is only prohibited if both parties acted with intent
options.c: The anticompetitive object alone suffices - for hardcore restrictions, no market analysis of actual effect is required
options.d: A 10% market-share de minimis threshold applies below which no review takes place

kartellrecht-grundlagen-02.explanation: Hardcore restrictions such as price-fixing, market/customer allocation, or bid-rigging are treated as "by object" restrictions of competition: a market-analysis defense ("there was no actual effect") is not available here - the anticompetitive object alone establishes the violation.

kartellrecht-grundlagen-03.question: Under Sec. 18(4) GWB, at what market share does the rebuttable presumption of single-firm dominance apply?

options.a: From 25 percent
options.b: From 40 percent
options.c: From 60 percent
options.d: Only from 75 percent

kartellrecht-grundlagen-03.explanation: Sec. 18(4) GWB presumes an undertaking to be dominant if it holds a market share of at least 40 percent - a rebuttable presumption, not an automatic violation. Sec. 18(5)-(6) additionally sets presumption thresholds for collective dominance (e.g. up to 3 undertakings with a combined 50% share, or up to 5 undertakings with a combined two-thirds share).

kartellrecht-grundlagen-04.question: A sales director informally discusses future price-increase plans with a competitor at an industry event, with no explicit agreement reached. Is this legally unproblematic?

options.a: Yes, without a written agreement there is never a cartel violation
options.b: No - exchanging future pricing intentions can itself constitute a prohibited "concerted practice" under Sec. 1 GWB, even without an explicit agreement
options.c: Yes, as long as no specific figures are mentioned
options.d: No, this is only relevant if more than three undertakings are involved

kartellrecht-grundlagen-04.explanation: Sec. 1 GWB expressly covers "concerted practices" - an explicit agreement is not required. Exchanging information about future (not merely past) pricing intentions with a competitor, even informally at an industry event, can itself constitute the prohibited coordination. This is precisely why trade-association meetings are treated as a classic cartel-risk scenario.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-01.question: Which of the following is NOT considered a classic hardcore restriction under competition law?

options.a: Price-fixing between competitors
options.b: Allocating customers or territories between competitors
options.c: An undertaking's unilateral internal decision to lower its own prices
options.d: Coordinated bids in public tenders (bid-rigging)

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-01.explanation: A unilateral internal pricing decision by one undertaking is simply normal competitive conduct, not an agreement or concerted practice between multiple undertakings - it lacks the necessary two-undertaking element of Sec. 1 GWB. Price-fixing, market/customer allocation, and bid-rigging, by contrast, are all recognized hardcore restrictions.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-02.question: In June 2025 the EU Commission fined Delivery Hero and Glovo EUR 329 million. What was this case about?

options.a: Excessive delivery prices charged to end customers
options.b: A cartel agreement not to poach each other's employees ("no-poach") and to allocate markets between the two companies
options.c: Data-protection violations related to food delivery
options.d: An unlawful merger that was never notified to the Commission

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-02.explanation: This was the EU Commission's first-ever decision on a pure labour-market cartel under Art. 101 TFEU: Delivery Hero and Glovo agreed not to poach each other's employees and additionally allocated national markets between themselves - even though Delivery Hero held only a minority stake in Glovo (i.e. not full merger-control-level control). No-poach agreements between competitors are therefore a confirmed, actively enforced cartel risk, not a theoretical edge case.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-03.question: In April 2025 the EU Commission fined 15 car manufacturers plus the industry association ACEA EUR 458 million. What made this cartel unusual?

options.a: It was a classic price-fixing agreement on new-car prices
options.b: For over 15 years, the manufacturers agreed not to advertise their vehicles' recyclability and not to compete on end-of-life-vehicle recycling payments - a cartel over non-competition on environmental information rather than price
options.c: It concerned an unlawful joint research cooperation on electric vehicles
options.d: The manufacturers agreed on common minimum warranty periods

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-03.explanation: This case shows cartels are not always about price: the manufacturers (VW receiving the largest individual amount, Mercedes-Benz obtaining full leniency immunity) agreed among themselves, for more than 15 years, not to advertise their vehicles' recyclability to customers and not to compete on end-of-life-vehicle recycling payments - an example of an information-suppression cartel under Art. 101 TFEU.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-04.question: Why are trade-association meetings considered a classic cartel-risk scenario?

options.a: Because trade associations are fundamentally prohibited under German law
options.b: Because they can involve informal exchanges of competitively sensitive information (e.g. future pricing intentions) between competitors, which can itself constitute a concerted practice
options.c: Because mere attendance at a trade-association meeting is automatically a cartel violation
options.d: Because trade-association meetings are only permitted for state-owned undertakings

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-04.explanation: The Bundeskartellamt publishes its own guidance on competition-law-compliant trade-association work precisely because this scenario is real: competitors regularly sit together at association meetings, and informal exchanges about future prices, capacity, or terms can - even without a formal resolution - constitute a prohibited concerted practice. Mere attendance is not itself a violation; what matters is the substance of what is exchanged.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-01.question: What is the statutory fine cap under Sec. 81c(2) GWB for serious competition-law violations?

options.a: EUR 1 million per violation, regardless of the undertaking's turnover
options.b: 10 percent of the worldwide total turnover of the entire corporate group in the preceding business year
options.c: 5 percent of the affected group's domestic German turnover
options.d: There is no statutory cap - the Bundeskartellamt decides freely

kartellrecht-bussgelder-01.explanation: Sec. 81c(2) GWB caps the fine at 10 percent of the total turnover achieved by the undertaking or association of undertakings in the preceding business year. Per Abs. 5, this means the worldwide turnover of the entire economic unit (corporate group), not just the individual participating legal entity. For less serious violations, Abs. 3 sets a lower 1% cap.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-02.question: What role does an effective compliance program play in fine assessment under Sec. 81d GWB?

options.a: A compliance program has no legal relevance whatsoever to the fine amount
options.b: Appropriate and effective precautions to prevent and detect violations - taken both before and after the offense - can be considered as a mitigating factor when assessing the fine
options.c: A compliance program automatically guarantees full immunity from fines
options.d: Only state-certified compliance programs may be taken into account

kartellrecht-bussgelder-02.explanation: Sec. 81d GWB (introduced by the 10th GWB amendment, 2021) expressly names "appropriate and effective precautions to prevent and detect violations" as a circumstance to be considered in fine assessment - both precautions taken before the violation and clarification/cooperation efforts afterward. This is a mitigation, not a guarantee: if the violation was orchestrated by company management itself, the mitigation effectively does not apply.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-03.question: In August 2026 the Bundeskartellamt fined six road-construction companies EUR 60.3 million for years of customer allocation and bid-rigging. How, per the Bundeskartellamt, did the companies disguise their price coordination?

options.a: They exclusively used encrypted email software
options.b: They met only once a year at an official trade fair
options.c: They met monthly in Kassel and used coded terms such as mileage readings, beer, or sausage prices as stand-ins for bid figures
options.d: The coordination was conducted exclusively through an intermediary lawyer

kartellrecht-bussgelder-03.explanation: In this case, competitors met monthly during the construction season in Kassel and communicated coordination by phone, email, or messenger using coded terms (mileage readings, beer or sausage prices, sponsorship amounts, hotel room rates) as cover for actual bid figures - a textbook example of how cartel coordination is disguised in practice. Alongside the corporate fine under Sec. 1 GWB, individuals involved are under investigation for possible bid-rigging under Sec. 298 StGB.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-04.question: What is the Bundeskartellamt's stance on "checkbox compliance" (mechanically ticking off as many measures as possible)?

options.a: It requires exactly 9 mandatory measures from every undertaking regardless of size
options.b: It mandates a fixed annual training requirement for all employees
options.c: It explicitly rejects mechanically implementing as many measures as possible, instead requiring a program genuinely tailored - and effective - relative to the undertaking's size, organization, and risk
options.d: It leaves it entirely up to undertakings whether a compliance program makes sense at all

kartellrecht-bussgelder-04.explanation: The Bundeskartellamt explicitly stresses that effective compliance does not consist of mechanically implementing as many measures as possible. It names nine flexible, non-mandatory "building blocks" (including risk analysis, tone from the top, staff training/selection, whistleblower systems) - but does not prescribe any specific training frequency or fixed review interval. This differs markedly from the GwG, which imposes an explicit ongoing training duty for anti-money-laundering compliance.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-01.question: What three requirements must an undertaking satisfy under Sec. 125(1) GWB to regain eligibility for public contracts despite a competition-law violation ("self-cleaning")?

options.a: Dismissal of management, payment of a state penalty, and dissolution of the affected department
options.b: Only full payment of the imposed fine
options.c: A public admission of guilt, an internal investigation, and an apology to competitors
options.d: Compensation for damage, comprehensive clarification of the facts through active cooperation, and concrete technical, organizational, and personnel measures to prevent future violations

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-01.explanation: Sec. 125(1) GWB cumulatively requires: (1) compensation for any damage caused by the offense, (2) comprehensive clarification of the facts and circumstances through active cooperation with the investigating authorities, and (3) concrete technical, organizational, and personnel measures suitable to prevent further violations. All three requirements must be satisfied together - none alone suffices.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-02.question: Where exactly does improved employee competition-law training fit within self-cleaning under Sec. 125 GWB?

options.a: It is a standalone-sufficient requirement, independent of the other two requirements
options.b: It falls under "personnel measures" (No. 3) - one of three requirements that must all be satisfied simultaneously, not sufficient on its own
options.c: It is not mentioned in the statute at all and is purely voluntary
options.d: It fully substitutes for the duty to compensate damage

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-02.explanation: Improved training falls under the "personnel measures" of Sec. 125(1) No. 3 GWB - alongside organizational and technical measures, a recognized category for preventing future violations. It is not sufficient alone, however: compensation for damage (No. 1) and comprehensive fact clarification through cooperation (No. 2) must also be satisfied.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-03.question: What must the contracting authority (or the Bundeskartellamt) do under Sec. 125(2) GWB if it considers the self-cleaning measures taken by the undertaking insufficient?

options.a: It may permanently exclude the undertaking from all tender procedures without further justification
options.b: It must give the undertaking the reasons for that decision
options.c: It must automatically initiate a new fine proceeding
options.d: It must submit the decision to a court for binding confirmation before it becomes effective

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-03.explanation: Sec. 125(2) GWB requires the contracting authority or the Bundeskartellamt to evaluate the measures taken, considering the severity and particular circumstances of the offense - if it considers them insufficient, it must give the undertaking the reasons for that decision - the statute does not prescribe a specific form (no explicit written-form requirement). This creates transparency and a basis for the undertaking to improve its measures or challenge the decision.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-04.question: What does self-cleaning under Sec. 125 GWB practically achieve - what can it exempt an undertaking from?

options.a: Payment of an already legally binding fine
options.b: A mandatory exclusion from public tender procedures that would otherwise apply under Sec. 123 or Sec. 124 GWB because of the competition-law violation
options.c: The individual criminal liability of involved persons under Sec. 298 StGB
options.d: The obligation to notify future mergers to the Bundeskartellamt

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-04.explanation: Sec. 125 GWB concerns the public-procurement side: an undertaking that would otherwise have to be excluded from public tender procedures under Sec. 123 or Sec. 124 GWB because of a competition-law violation can regain its eligibility through successful self-cleaning. The fine itself, and any individual criminal liability under Sec. 298 StGB, remain unaffected by this.

kartellrecht-straftaten-01.question: What criminal consequence does an individual face under Sec. 298 StGB for submitting a tender offer based on an unlawful agreement?

options.a: Only a fine of at most EUR 1,000
options.b: Imprisonment of up to 5 years, or a fine
options.c: Mandatorily at least 2 years' imprisonment without suspension
options.d: No criminal consequences at all - only the involved undertakings can be held liable

kartellrecht-straftaten-01.explanation: Sec. 298 StGB (bid-rigging in public tenders) criminalizes submitting a tender offer based on an unlawful (cartel) agreement - imprisonment of up to 5 years, or a fine (Abs. 1). Abs. 2 extends this to negotiated-award procedures following a prior competitive process. This is individual criminal liability, in addition to the corporate fine under the GWB.

kartellrecht-straftaten-02.question: What possibility does Sec. 298(3) StGB provide for a person who was involved in a bid-rigging agreement but voluntarily reverses it?

options.a: No such possibility exists under the statute
options.b: Automatic exemption from punishment through mere subsequent regret, without further action
options.c: Exemption from punishment if the person voluntarily prevents the rigged offer's acceptance, or voluntarily and genuinely attempts to do so
options.d: Only a 50% reduction in sentence, never full exemption from punishment

kartellrecht-straftaten-02.explanation: Sec. 298(3) StGB contains a voluntary-withdrawal provision: a person who voluntarily prevents the rigged offer's acceptance, or genuinely and seriously attempts to do so, remains exempt from punishment. This requires active conduct - mere internal regret without action does not suffice.

kartellrecht-straftaten-03.question: Unlike money-laundering law (GwG), is there a statutorily fixed minimum frequency for competition-law compliance training?

options.a: Yes, at least once a year for all customer-facing employees
options.b: No - neither the GWB nor the Bundeskartellamt's administrative practice prescribes a specific training frequency; expectations scale to the undertaking's size, structure, and risk
options.c: Yes, every two years under a binding EU directive
options.d: No, training is entirely irrelevant in competition law and is never taken into account

kartellrecht-straftaten-03.explanation: Unlike Sec. 6(2) No. 6 GwG (which prescribes an explicit, ongoing training duty for anti-money-laundering compliance), competition law has no fixed, statutorily mandated training frequency. The Bundeskartellamt assesses the effectiveness of a compliance program - including training - case by case, based on the undertaking's size, structure, and risk profile, not on a rigid calendar interval.

kartellrecht-straftaten-04.question: In the road-construction cartel case, four of the involved companies received a reduction in their fine. Through which instrument is such a reduction typically achieved?

options.a: Through an out-of-court settlement directly with the harmed customers
options.b: Through the leniency program (Bonusregelung) - an undertaking that discloses its involvement in a cartel and actively cooperates with the authorities can receive a fine reduction or full immunity
options.c: By proving that competition was not actually affected in practice
options.d: By making a voluntary additional payment to the state treasury

kartellrecht-straftaten-04.explanation: The Bundeskartellamt's leniency program (Bonusregelung) rewards undertakings that are first to disclose their cartel involvement and cooperate comprehensively with a fine reduction, up to and including full immunity. In the road-construction case, four companies obtained a reduction this way - a strong incentive to self-report violations early rather than conceal them.
